01.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to declare, say'. The form is tagged imperfect, but this verb's past forms serve in narrative simply as 'said'.

02.r: The man Jesus is speaking with.

03.r: Greek often puts the article before a personal name; English does not.

05.r: Opens a condition the man is free to accept.

06.r: The man's own will is appealed to.
06.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to will, be willing, wish, desire'. The YLT's 'thou dost will' keeps the plain present.

07.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from τέλος, 'end', and gives 'having reached its end, finished, mature, complete, perfect'. The sense is completeness, reaching the goal, more than flawlessness.

08.r: The state he wants to reach.

09.r: The first of a string of commands.
09.n: A present imperative, set straight against the aorist 'sell' with no 'and' between them.

10.n: An aorist imperative: a single, decisive act.

12.r: With the participle that follows, makes a noun: the things that belong to you.

13.n: Literally 'the things being at hand', a participle used as a noun. Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses this phrase for Hebrew words for property and livestock, such as מִקְנֶה.

14.r: Joins the giving to the selling.

15.r: Give the money from the sale.
15.n: The Greek gives no object; the Geneva supplies 'it'.

16.r: The article; 'to' comes from the dative case of the noun.
16.n: The Textus Receptus lacks this article; the English is unaffected.

17.r: Those who have nothing and depend on others.
17.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from a verb meaning 'to crouch, cower': first a beggar, one who crouches and cowers, then poor in general.

19.r: A promise attached to the commands.

22.n: Plural in our text, without an article; English needs 'the'. The Textus Receptus has the singular, 'heaven', which all six translations use.

24.r: A call to come to Jesus.
24.n: Properly an adverb, 'here, hither'. Abbott-Smith notes its use as an imperative, 'here! come!', and cites this verse.

25.r: A call to go with Jesus as his disciple.
25.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to accompany, follow', and as a figurative sense 'of discipleship'. A present imperative: an ongoing following.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus reads οὐρανῷ, 'heaven' (singular), where our text has the plural 'heavens'; the KJV's 'in heaven' follows it. It also lacks the article before 'poor', which makes no difference in English.
